new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., text present; also rendered p.1 and p.3 as images). Page 3, heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', reads exactly: 'Stress is not phonemic, occurring on the final syllable of the word.' / 'There are two phonemic tones; high [ ] and low [ ].' followed by the tone minimal pairs àrì 'people' / árí 'sun', èr 'tree' / ér 'arrow' (grave/acute diacritics visible in the page scan; the bracketed tone-mark glyphs did not survive the text, which is the only difference from the reported quote). Same page, 'Conventions: Phonological': '/e/ and /i/ have centralized allophones in unstressed syllables contiguous to nasals and when the vowel is nasalized'; p.4: 'phonemic tone is not…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the word-final syllable; the language additionally has a two-way (high vs low) lexical tone contrast (Irwin 1974: intonation overrides word tone in sentences; tone not written in the orthography).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only other stress-related remark (OPD p.3 = Irwin 1974 p.4) is that /e/ and /i/ have centralised allophones in unstressed syllables contiguous to nasals
new_statements.domain_note: stated for 'the word'; examples are citation forms. Irwin 1974 p.5 adds that sentence intonation perturbs word tones. Tida 2011 analyses the Simbu group (incl. a Salt variety, 'Salt-Kia') as word-melody tone languages, so the 'final stress' may be a phonetic prominence co-existing with word tone.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD sheet is titled 'Salt-Yui (Salt-Iui) Language [SLL], Salt – Chimbu Province', villages Diani, Dirima, Oirima, Gomri, Abai — i.e. the Yui variety Irwin worked on (Glottolog salt1242; Glottolog lists sub-varieties Salt [salt1245] and Keri [keri1251]). Irwin 1974 calls the language simply 'Yui'. Tida 2011's own data are from 'Salt-Kia', a Salt-area variety, not necessarily Irwin's Yui.

sources.note: Sec. 0.4 Sound System (pp.4-5) is brief: vowels, consonants, and 0.4.3 Tone ('Two contrastive tones occur in Yui designated high/low: ari people vs ari sun, er tree vs er arrow'; 'Intonation overrides the tone patterns of individual words in sentences.. Tone has been omitted in the writing of this grammar'). Stress is mentioned only in passing ('unstressed syllables contiguous to nasals'); no statement of where stress falls. Refers readers to his typescript 'Salt-Yui Phonology', 1967, for the full analysis.

sources.note: p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Stress is not phonemic, occurring on the final syllable of the word. There are two phonemic tones; high and low' with minimal pairs ari 'people'/'sun', er 'tree'/'arrow'; p.3 also notes /e/,/i/ centralised in unstressed syllables next to nasals; p.4 'phonemic tone is not written'.

sources.citation: Tida, Syuntarô [千田俊太郎]. 2011. 東シンブー諸語サブグルーピングに向けて [Towards subgrouping of East Simbu languages]. 地球研言語記述論集 3: 153-182.
sources.note: Comparative (Japanese). Sec. 2.4: 'the Simbu languages are probably all tone languages, with word-domain melodies contrastive' (high/falling/rising/low/key-lowering); gives own tone data for a Salt variety ('Salt-Kia'); remarks that Irwin (1974) noticed tone is distinctive in Yui but gave only two or three examples and no analysis. Nothing on stress placement in Yui.
